output.title: Retrieval quality is a workflow constraint, not a nice-to-have
output.body:
If your AI tool or automation has to look up information to do useful work, retrieval quality is part of the workflow design, not an afterthought. In plain terms: when the system searches documents, emails, FAQs, or past records, it has to pull back the right material consistently, or the answer looks neat and is still wrong. That creates rework for you, or worse, a confident mistake. For a small business, the useful question is not “can AI answer this?” but “can it find the right source every time this task runs?”

A practical rule of thumb: if one recurring task needs you to search more than one place for the answer, retrieval quality has become a design constraint. That could be customer questions, invoice checks, or lead follow-up. Before automating anything, audit the source material for that one task. Are the documents named clearly, grouped sensibly, and kept current? If the inputs are messy, automation usually moves the manual work earlier, not away.

One control I would keep is source display: the system should show which document it used before you trust the answer. Bareni’s own local knowledge-assistant demo shows grounded answers with sources on synthetic data, but the public route is locked, so treat that as a demo pattern, not a deployed service. The next step is simple: pick one repeating workflow and check whether the information is organised well enough to retrieve before you try to automate it.
